Newborn Care

Infantile hemangiomas: which birthmarks need early care?

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

At three weeks, a spot on your baby’s cheek looks redder and more raised than it did in a photo from the hospital. That change is worth showing the clinician who cares for your baby. One possible explanation is an infantile hemangioma, a benign growth of blood vessels. How fast it is changing, where it sits and whether it affects feeding, vision or breathing help determine the next step.

Which mark are you looking at?

An infantile hemangioma may be barely visible at birth and become clearer during the first few weeks. Near the surface it can look like a raised red patch. A deeper one may look like a soft swelling with a bluish hue. A clinician usually identifies it by examining the skin and asking how it has changed.

A flat pink patch over an eyelid, between the eyebrows or at the back of the neck is often a different vascular birthmark called a salmon patch. The term “angel kiss” commonly refers to a salmon patch on the face. A mark that starts to thicken, grows quickly or affects the eyelid needs assessment whatever name someone first gave it.

Why the first weeks matter

Growth is often fastest between about one and three months of age. Researchers who examined serial family photographs of 30 infants with facial hemangiomas saw rapid changes during the early weeks. This small, selected group illustrates how much can happen between appointments. It cannot predict how a particular baby’s mark will grow.

After the growth phase, many hemangiomas flatten and fade gradually over several years. Some leave loose skin, fine visible vessels or a scar. Taking a dated photograph under similar lighting and at a similar distance can help your clinician compare visits. Call about rapid change instead of waiting until you have a series of pictures.

Which marks should be assessed promptly?

Contact your baby’s clinician early about a growing mark near an eye, on the nose or lip, or one that covers a broad area of the face. Even a small eyelid growth can interfere with vision. A lip lesion can make feeding painful. Skin that breaks down, especially around the mouth or diaper area, can form a painful sore called an ulcer. Tell the team if the baby’s intake drops or an open area develops.

If you count five or more suspected skin hemangiomas, tell the clinician how many you see. They may recommend an ultrasound to check the liver. A single uncomplicated mark can often be assessed without a scan. For a potentially high-risk hemangioma, the American Academy of Pediatrics advises early specialist assessment, ideally by one month of age. If your baby is already older, contact the team as soon as you notice the concern.

What observation and treatment involve

For a small, low-risk growth, ask when the next examination should happen and what change would bring it forward. If a mark threatens vision, feeding, breathing or lasting changes to the skin, a specialist may offer medicine during the growth phase. Oral propranolol is a usual first choice when whole-body treatment is needed. It requires a prescription, an assessment and an individual plan for feeds, illness and monitoring.

A topical beta blocker may be appropriate for selected thin, superficial lesions. Laser treatment or surgery has a role in some cases, including for changes left after growth subsides. Ask what each option aims to protect and what improvement is realistic. If others ask about a visible mark, a simple explanation such as “It’s a blood-vessel birthmark our clinician is following” is enough if you want to answer.

If the skin opens or bleeds

Ask your clinician how to protect an ulcer and control pain. If the mark bleeds, press a clean cloth or gauze directly on it without lifting it repeatedly to check. Great Ormond Street Hospital advises urgent care if bleeding continues beyond ten minutes of pressure. Seek emergency help sooner for heavy bleeding, significant difficulty breathing, or a baby who looks very unwell.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Record when the mark appeared and how it changes.

Arrange prompt review of high-risk locations, sores or multiple marks.

Ask about follow-up and the goal of any recommended treatment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests bringing a dated picture and a short note on feeding, comfort or eyelid opening. These observations help a clinician judge what the change means for your baby.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for significant breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or a very unwell baby. A bleeding mark that continues after ten minutes of steady pressure needs urgent care.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Show your baby’s clinician a growing vascular mark early, particularly on the face.
  • Ask whether location, the number of lesions or an open sore changes the follow-up plan.
  • Even a mark that will eventually fade can affect vision, feeding or the skin during the growth phase.

Frequently asked questions

When does an infantile hemangioma appear?

It often becomes apparent in the first weeks, sometimes at the site of a faint patch seen at birth. Its change in thickness and size can help a clinician distinguish it from a flat salmon patch.

What causes the blood vessels to grow?

The exact cause is unclear. Infantile hemangiomas are more common in babies born preterm or at a lower birth weight. These associations cannot explain why an individual baby has one or attribute it to something a parent did.

Will it disappear on its own?

Many shrink and lighten over several years. The skin can still have a different texture or fine visible vessels afterward. A clinician can discuss what to expect based on the mark’s location, thickness and growth.

Does a baby always need treatment?

Many small low-risk lesions need observation alone. Early specialist advice is important for a rapidly changing facial mark, a sore, trouble feeding, or a growth that could affect vision or breathing. Breathing difficulty needs emergency attention.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
